Hydro-Morphodynamic Behaviors of the Mahanadi River system: A Multi-temporal Satellite and Experimental Study

Abstract:

Deltaic drainage networks evolve under the combined influence of structural inheritance, sedimentary processes, and episodic channel reorganization. This study examines the drainage architecture of the Mahanadi Delta using an integrated morphometric and fractal framework to assess how internal network organization interacts with external geomorphic controls. Drainage networks were extracted from SRTM digital elevation data and analysed using stream-order based morphometric indices and box-counting fractal analysis. The resulting fractal dimension (D &asymp 1.23) indicates a moderately complex non&ndashspace-filling network geometry typical of low-relief, sediment-dominated deltaic plains. Along with the persistence of turbulence structures across successive bends remains one of the least understood aspects of sinuous channel hydraulics. This study investigates the three-dimensional turbulence dynamics and nonlinear flow behaviour in a sinuous open-channel flow using detailed velocity measurements collected at seven cross-sections spanning bend apexes and crossover regions. Mean velocity components, turbulence intensities, Reynolds shear stresses, turbulence length scales, Lyapunov exponents, Average Mutual Information, autocorrelation functions, Poincar&eacute sections, and radial density distributions were analyzed to examine the evolution of flow structures over multiple sinuous wavelengths. The results reveal a strong interaction between curvature-induced secondary circulation, momentum redistribution, and coherent turbulent structures throughout the channel. Turbulence length-scale analyses show progressive growth and downstream persistence of coherent vortices, while nonlinear dynamical analyses reveal deterministic chaotic behaviour characterized by positive Lyapunov exponents, elevated mutual information, and evolving attractor geometries. The strongest spatial variability occurs within the intermediate flow region, where secondary circulation is most developed and turbulence organization is most pronounced. These findings demonstrate that turbulence in sinuous channels behaves as a spatially connected dynamical system rather than a sequence of independent bend-scale events.
